clinicalPearls: A common, benign inflammatory condition of the tongue seen at any age
Presents as well-demarcated red areas of depapillation surrounded by slightly raised, serpiginous white or yellowish borders
The lesions characteristically change shape and location over days to weeks, giving a migrating map-like appearance
Usually asymptomatic, though some patients report soreness or sensitivity to spicy, acidic, or hot foods
Frequently coexists with a fissured tongue and has recognised associations with psoriasis and atopy
The diagnosis is clinical, based on the characteristic appearance and migratory behaviour, and biopsy is rarely needed
There is no malignant potential, and reassurance is the cornerstone of management
Symptomatic patients benefit from avoiding trigger foods and, when needed, topical symptomatic measures
reference.pathophysiology: Geographic tongue is a benign inflammatory disorder in which localised loss of the filiform papillae produces smooth red patches, while the advancing margins show a band of inflammatory cells and regenerating epithelium seen clinically as a raised white-yellow border. Histologically the changes resemble those of psoriasis, with collections of neutrophils in the epithelium, and the condition shares associations with psoriasis and atopic disease. The lesions resolve and reappear in new sites, which accounts for the shifting, map-like pattern; the precise trigger is unknown but immune and possibly genetic factors are implicated.
additionalDifferentials: Glossitis from nutritional deficiency of iron, vitamin B12, or folate
Erythroplakia, a red patch requiring exclusion of dysplasia
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on the characteristic migratory appearance
Review for associated fissured tongue and any personal or family history of psoriasis or atopy
Haematinics (ferritin, vitamin B12, folate) if glossitis or soreness suggests deficiency
Candidal swab or smear if fungal infection is suspected
Biopsy only in atypical, persistent, or non-migratory lesions to exclude other pathology
Photographic documentation to demonstrate the changing pattern
redFlags: A fixed, non-migrating red patch that could represent erythroplakia and needs biopsy
Persistent soreness with systemic symptoms suggesting nutritional deficiency or another disorder
Induration, ulceration, or bleeding not typical of geographic tongue
Widespread candidiasis raising concern about immunosuppression
reference.prognosis: The condition is entirely benign with an excellent prognosis; lesions wax and wane over time and may persist for years, but they cause no harm and require no active treatment beyond reassurance and symptomatic relief.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for candidiasis and giving unnecessary antifungal treatment
Failing to distinguish a fixed red lesion, a possible erythroplakia, from migratory patches
Overlooking a treatable nutritional deficiency in a sore tongue
Causing undue alarm by suggesting a risk of malignancy where none exists
references: Cawson's Essentials of Oral Pathology and Oral Medicine
management: Reassure that geographic tongue is benign, self-limiting, and needs no active treatment
Advise avoidance of provoking foods such as spicy, acidic, salty, or hot items when lesions are sore
Offer symptomatic relief with topical anaesthetic, antihistamine, or anti-inflammatory mouthrinses, and topical corticosteroids for troublesome soreness
Correct any coexisting haematinic deficiency of iron, vitamin B12, or folate contributing to glossitis
Treat superimposed candidal infection with a topical antifungal if it develops
Re-examine or biopsy atypical, persistent, or non-migratory lesions to exclude other pathology

cells.text: Asymptomatic inflammatory condition with rapid loss and regrowth of filiform papillae, giving denuded red patches that wander across the tongue surface.

Elongated filiform papillae of the medial dorsal surface because the keratin layer fails to desquamate normally; brownish-black color may come from staining by tobacco, food, or chromogenic organisms.
Appearance in scarlet fever from hypertrophy of fungiform papillae plus changes in filiform papillae.

Atrophy that may be associated with xerostomia, pernicious anemia, iron-deficiency anemia, pellagra, or syphilis; may cause painful burning; may reflect erythematous candidiasis and respond to antifungals.
